passage:
I'm Chetan, and for most of last year my phone rang at midnight. It was always Pooja, my oldest friend from college, and it was always someone: the landlord who hated her, the team lead who ruined her life, the cousin who betrayed her. Some of it was surely real. Some of it had been going on since we were nineteen.
One night she said, "You're the only one I have, and even you don't care." I felt the old guilt rise. Then I tried something new. I listened for ten minutes without fixing. Then I asked, "That sounds painful. What do you want to do about it?"
Silence. Then: "I don't know. Maybe talk to HR."
"Good start. And Pooja, I care, but I can't do calls after eleven any more. Sunday lunches, though, I'm always in."
She was cold for a week. Then she came to Sunday lunch and told me what HR said.

qa.q: After what time did Chetan say the calls could no longer happen?
qa.a: Chetan said the calls could not happen after eleven any more.

qa.q: What did Chetan feel when Pooja said "even you don't care"?
qa.a: Chetan felt the old guilt rise, the familiar pull to prove care by giving in.

qa.q: Which question at the turning point changed the call, and why?
qa.a: Asking "What do you want to do about it?" after listening moved Pooja from blaming to thinking of a step, like talking to HR, without Chetan taking on her problem.

qa.q: How might Pooja have experienced Chetan's new limit?
qa.a: At first she felt rejected, which is why she was cold for a week, but the Sunday lunch offer showed she still mattered, so she came back and shared her progress.

grounding: A person listens kindly to an old friend's constant stories of being wronged, asks what she wants to do, and holds a firm limit on late-night calls.

passage:
Team lead's notes, weekly check-in, 12 August
Watched Manoj handle a hard moment with Vinita today, and I want to record it.
Vinita had missed the vendor deadline. When Manoj asked about it at stand-up, she said, "Of course it's my fault. It's always my fault. Nobody here knows what I'm dealing with at home." The room went quiet.
Manoj didn't argue, and didn't back down. He said, "I'm sorry things are hard at home. That sounds heavy. What would help you get the file out by Friday?" When she said he should just do it, he said, "I can't take it on this week, but I can sit with you for twenty minutes after lunch to plan it."
They met after lunch. The file went out Thursday.
Action: remind Vinita privately about the staff support line. Tell Manoj this was well handled.

qa.q: When did the file go out?
qa.a: The file went out Thursday.

qa.q: What might Vinita have been feeling when she said "It's always my fault"?
qa.a: She seemed overwhelmed and defensive, perhaps ashamed about the missed deadline and weighed down by what she was dealing with at home.

qa.q: Which part of Manoj's reply held the boundary without dismissing her?
qa.a: He acknowledged her hard time and asked what would help, then refused to take on the work while offering twenty minutes to plan, which respected her pain but kept the task hers.

qa.q: How does the team lead see Manoj's handling?
qa.a: The team lead thinks it is worth recording and plans to praise it, seeing that calm, kind firmness got the file out while support for Vinita was arranged separately.

grounding: A team lead records how Manoj met Vinita's cry of always being blamed with kindness and a firm limit, and how the work still got done.

passage:
Wednesday night
Chinmay called again at eleven. Forty minutes. His landlord is cheating him. His boss is jealous of him. His sister never calls. And tonight, somehow, it was also my fault, because I "never really help."
I listened. I do care about him. Some of it is real. His boss does sound difficult.
But I've noticed I end every call feeling guilty for things that aren't mine.
So tonight, near the end, I asked him something new. "Chinmay, what do you want to do about the landlord? Is there a step you want to take?" He went quiet. Then he said, "I don't know. Maybe look for a new flat."
Then I said, kindly, "I want to keep being your friend. But I can't take calls after ten on weeknights anymore. I'm exhausted. Sundays are good."
He sighed. I didn't apologise. I said goodnight.
Salma

qa.q: What time did Chinmay call?
qa.a: At eleven.

qa.q: How does Salma feel at the end of Chinmay's calls?
qa.a: Salma feels guilty and exhausted, taking on blame for things that don't belong to Salma.

qa.q: What did Salma do that shows compassion with boundaries?
qa.a: She listened, asked what Chinmay wanted to do about the landlord, and kindly set a limit of no calls after ten on weeknights.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel when Salma sets the limit?
qa.a: Chinmay may feel a little hurt or disappointed, which is why he sighs, but he was also given a real question to think about.

grounding: A diary shows an adult listening kindly to a friend's complaints, asking what he wants to do, and staying firm about personal limits.

passage:
In the village near Satara, Usha had barely put down her water pot when her sister-in-law Madhuri started again.
"Nobody in this house cares about me. Aai criticises my cooking. Your brother never takes my side. And you, Usha, you just watch."
Usha sat on the step beside her. She could see Madhuri's eyes were red. Some of it was real. Aai did criticise her cooking, loudly, in front of guests.
"That sounds hard," Usha said. "I've heard how Aai talks at dinner. It isn't fair."
Madhuri blinked. She'd expected an argument.
"What do you want to do about it?" Usha asked. "Do you want to talk to her? Or to my brother first?"
"I want you to tell Aai."
"I can sit with you when you talk to her. But I won't fight your fight for you, and I'm not the one who hurt you."
Madhuri was quiet. Then, slowly, "Sit with me tomorrow, then."

qa.q: What did Madhuri say Aai criticises?
qa.a: Aai criticises her cooking.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling as she sat beside Madhuri?
qa.a: Usha felt sympathetic, seeing Madhuri's red eyes and knowing some of the hurt was real, but calm and clear that the blame was not hers.

qa.q: How did Usha show compassion while keeping her limits?
qa.a: Usha agreed that the criticism was unfair, asked what Madhuri wanted to do, offered to sit with her, but refused to fight her fight or accept blame.

qa.q: How did Madhuri react to Usha's kindness?
qa.a: Madhuri was surprised, expecting an argument, and then agreed to talk to Aai with Usha beside her.

grounding: It shows an adult listening kindly to a sister-in-law's pain, asking what she wants to do, and holding her own limits.

passage: Rain streaked the window of the café in Malmö while Anders talked for forty minutes. His boss was unfair, his ex had turned their friends against him, and now Emil, of all people, had "abandoned" him by not covering his weekend shifts at the bike shop. Emil listened, nodding, stirring a cold coffee. Anders was genuinely low; his eyes were puffy and his jacket hadn't been washed in a while. When Anders finally paused, Emil said, "That sounds like a rough month. I'm sorry. What do you want to do about the job?" Anders blinked. "I mean... if you'd just take Saturday..." "I can't do Saturdays, I told you that. I can help you write to your boss about the schedule tonight, if you want." Anders looked annoyed, then tired. "Fine. Tonight." Emil paid for both coffees and felt steadier than usual walking home.

qa.q: How long did Anders talk at the café?
qa.a: Anders talked for forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Emil feel walking home?
qa.a: Emil felt steadier than usual, having shown real care without giving up the limit on Saturdays.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Anders what he wanted to do and offering to help write to his boss respected his pain while keeping Emil's limit on Saturday shifts.

qa.q: How did Anders take being refused?
qa.a: Anders looked annoyed, then tired, but agreed to write to his boss, which suggests part of him was ready to act.

grounding: Shows a person listening kindly, asking what the other wants to do, and staying firm about their own limits without accepting blame.
